text:
When I obtained a new computer, I realized almost to my horror that with the way the GPU would be suspended within the case, there was a genuine potential for the card to sag under its own weight and potentially ruin the card or the case. This is not something you really want to think about when you spend thousands of dollars on a computer system, so I immediately took to various sites for recommendations for ways to support the GPU and eventually, I stumbled upon this little thing.

I will admit that I was a bit skeptical at first when I received it. The item itself doesn't really look like much, and despite feeling fairly sturdy, I wasn't sure how well it would do in the case itself or if it would even be that supportive.

Turns out I was worried for nothing.

The head being telescopic means it can neatly and snugly fit between the bottom of your GPU and the case regardless of the height, and once it's in there, it is IN THERE. Neither the support or the card are going to move. The trickiest part was attempting to figure out where to position it so it wouldn't get in the way of the GPU's fans. With my particular card, sticking it beneath one of the corners closest to the fans along the front of the case it's in made the most sense, but your particular situation may vary.

I've had this thing for several months now and have not noticed the GPU sagging or any similar issues, so I'm quite happily calling this one a win for now.

Additionally, vastly improved performance on DX11 and DX9 titles. This is easily the best affordable entry into PC gaming anyone could buy. If that sounds like a headache, go with NVIDIA or AMD (not the 6000 series, AMD while not cancelling support - they sure did show their hand when they attempted to do just that).

Regardless of the strides they’ve made with the drivers this isn’t good for anything using Direct X 11 and not being able to play older titles is a major drawback to this card.

Which is a shame because like I said Intel has come far in a short amount of time. XeSS is actually more useful in most games than FSR ever was before 3.1. Even to the point of make the cards performance actually rival an RTX 4060 Ti at times. So if you’re looking at this and think you can make use of this card just make sure you aren’t interested in older software. Also make sure you have a newer CPU to push this GPU because the tests Hardware Unboxed conducted were spot on. This GPU does not like old or low level CPUs.

Sadly, I couldn’t use this card in the end, but I genuinely want Intel to keep making GPUs because the PC community need something to cause a ruckus in the GPU landscape. It’d be nice to see NVIDIA and AMD to be competitive again.

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I bought this card to replace a Quadro P2000. I selected this card rather than a more upscale card because it didn’t require a separate power cable and only filled two PCiE slots. (There appears to be a shortage of double width cards because of nvidia’s forthcoming 5000 series.) The card is now functioning well and an improvement over my old card. However I noticed several peculiarities that are worth mentioning.

The card is listed as an nvidia card. While that is true, the manufacturer of the card I received was PNY. In terms of quality, PNY. while a satisfactory manufacturer, is considered at the lower end by most reviewers. It still uses an nvidia chip set.

When I ordered this card the price was $465. When I came back to the site the next day it was $480. Is this older card subject to dynamic pricing?

There was no instruction sheet in the package.

The filler bracket attached was a short height one, but a full height one was in the package. I tried to change to the full height one, but found it was attached with TORX screws. My T3 screwdriver was too small and my T10 too large. The PNY web site said the screws were T5. Luckily I ordered a full set of inexpensive TORX screwdrivers, because two screws were T5 and two T8. Given the likelihood of people changing the bracket, it would have been nice to have included two inexpensive TORX screwdrivers (or even better, using different screw heads).

When I installed the nvidia drivers, they automatically switched my sound drivers to an nvidia sound driver which I had to disable to select a default sound driver that matched my sound card.

None of this affects the performance of the card, which appears to have speeded up my Premiere Pro.

text:
La MSI RTX 4060 Ti è una scheda grafica di fascia media che NVIDIA progettata per offrire buone prestazioni a 1080p e 1440p senza un costo eccessivo.

Questa variante Msi Gaming X offre Rgb molto bello da vedere e un ottima dissipazione restando silenziosa.

Ecco i punti principali da considerare:

1. Prestazioni

La RTX 4060 Ti si basa sull’architettura Ada Lovelace e offre una buona performance in giochi moderni a 1080p, con frame rate costanti e dettagli elevati.

A risoluzioni di 1440p, mantiene comunque prestazioni valide, anche se con alcuni giochi più pesanti potrebbe richiedere l'abbassamento dei dettagli per mantenere frame rate fluidi.

Grazie al DLSS 3, disponibile su questa serie, è possibile migliorare ulteriormente le prestazioni nei giochi che supportano questa tecnologia. Il DLSS 3 permette di aumentare i frame senza sacrificare troppo la qualità dell'immagine, soprattutto per chi gioca a risoluzioni maggiori.

2. Efficienza Energetica

Il consumo energetico della RTX 4060 Ti è relativamente basso rispetto a schede di generazioni precedenti, grazie alla nuova architettura e all'ottimizzazione dei consumi, con un TDP di circa 160W. Questo rende la scheda adatta anche a sistemi con alimentatori di media potenza.

Le MSIGaming X sono progettate per un raffreddamento efficiente, con ventole Torx di ultima generazione e un sistema di dissipazione che aiuta a mantenere temperature stabili anche durante sessioni di gioco prolungate.

text:
Had an old gtx 1080ti gpu and naturally was starting to show its age (the fact it lasted so long shows how great a gpu it was, and depending on use still is). I decided to upgrade. I was contemplating getting this or an AMD gpu. I got this because it's Nvidia and the driver support is much better than AMD. I have a PCIE 3.0 motherboard and this requires a PCIE 4.0 motherboard (PCIE is backward compatible so the latest gpu will even work on a PCIE 1.0 port). I decided to get this anyway as it's only 1 generation below and I am essentially loosing 5-10fps which is nothing massively different (essentially with each generation you will be loosing no more than 5-10fps, depending on the system it is added to; so each newer generaton would near enough double by this amount). I only need to upgrade the motherboard if it is 2 generations or more above, as than the performance is noticeable (much lower fps and slower texture pop-in and the like). I got the rtx 4060ti 16gb gpu (won't go anything lower with vram since 8gb should be the least of it nowadays and 11gb the standard due to how demanding applications are today).

Having got it, benchmarked it and tested it in various ways I can safely say it is a great card. I got it and benchmarked it natively (without dlss or any performance support) at maximum settings "by todays standards" getting near 24-30fps on the lowest and about 33-50fps on average (obviously anything older will be much higher). I take it if I had a PCIE 4.0 port I would get an extra 5-10fps. So anywhere from 29-55fps at maximum settings. This gpu can handle pretty much anything thrown at it and with the addition of adding frame generation an extra 30-40fps is gained on max settings. Also it's nice that this gpu is doing all this and using near half of what my 1080ti used in terms of power. Which saves some money with electricity bills. The one issue I have is the 128 bit bottleneck, which they should have made it at least 192 bits as performance would largely have been increased. But this is understandable as this would have used more power to do so. The gpu is incredibly efficient and does alot with what it has. It stays cool and quiet pretty much all the time even in demanding situations. Has "incredible" overclocking potential considering its only using 1 pcie x8 connector for power; this is very impressive but as said limited by the 128bit memory bandwidth. It is very efficient with what it has.

The gpu is really a 1-2k card, and can go 4k depending on the application used, though if incredibly demanding will require frame generation which adds so much fps it is unreal. Overall a great gpu, as if you are upgrading from a 1080ti like me a big leap in terms of performance but if you are coming from a 3080ti the leap is nothing major besides adding frame generation (unless you specifically want this feature; but will depend on application support). So anything below a 3080ti is worth an upgrade. Only 4x/5x nvidia gpu cards can do true frame generation because of an Optical Flow Accelerator and newer tensor cores (AMD has their version but is largely inferior due to lack of hardware support and being "mostly driver based"). As said adding frame generation provides so much of a performance boost it is unreal (anywhere from 30-40-fps). Overall a great card, though my only gripe is could be a little cheaper. That is the only issue with the gpu, they should have made it cheaper to reflect its performance (as in native performance without frame generation or dlss). Overall though, a great gpu.

text:
MSI 4070 SUPER OC Ventus 2X’i Amazon.com.tr satıcısından aldım. Öncelikle her zamanki gibi özenli paketleme ve hızlı kargo teslimatı için teşekkürlerimi iletiyorum. Orijinal kapalı kutusunda geldi. ATX 3.0 standardına uygun PSU’nuz yoksa, kutu içinde 2x8-pin güç kablosunu +12VHPWR’a dönüştüren bir kablo çıkıyor.
MSI’in Ventus 2X fanlı modelini alırken çok ısınma problemi yaşar mıyım diye herkes gibi ben de düşündüm. Ama; hem yeni nesil uzun ekran kartlarına uyumlu olmayan eski tip kasamın olması, hem de monitörümün 1920 x 1080 / 60 Hz olması nedeniyle (kısa vadede 2K veya 4K monitör almayı düşünmediğimden) 1080p’de sorun olmayacağını düşünerek bu kartı sipariş verdim. İlk izlenimlerim beni pişman etmeyecek gibi. Oyunlarda 1080p Ultra ayarlarda sorun yaşatmayacak gibi görünüyor.
Şu ana kadar test ettiğim en yüksek sistem gereksinimi isteyen oyun “Portal with RTX” oldu. 1080p + DLSS + RTX + Ultra ayarlarda yaklaşık 1 saatlik oynama sonrası çıkan değerleri yazıyorum: Kart sıcaklığı ort 76 - max 80 / Kart Hotspot sıcaklığı ort 87 - max 91 / FPS ort 120 - min 105 / kart fan hızı ort 2.200 rpm - max 2.500 rpm / TDP ise üreticinin belirlediği max değer olan 220 watt civarında / kart Core Clock ort 2.760 MHz - max 2.865 MHz (MSI Afterburner’dan OC’li).
MSI Afterburner ile çok stabil, risksiz ve kolayca OC yapılabiliyor. 4070 SUPER’in üretici standart Core Clock değeri 2.475 MHz, MSI’in bu modeli OC’li olduğundan 2.505 MHz (+1%) olarak geliyor. Ama MSI Afterburner ile sorunsuz OC yapınca yaklaşık +15% Core Clock (+360 MHz) artışı ile 2.865 MHz olarak kullanıyorum. Tabi bu 80 derecelere ulaşan kart sıcaklıklarına ve 90 derecelere ulaşan Hostpot sıcaklıklarına neden oluyor. OC’siz %100 GPU kullanımında bu sıcaklık değerleri ortalama 70-75 derece ve 80-85 derece olacaktır yine.
Furmark 1 ve Furmark 2 ile yaptığım sentetik testlerde sırasıyla 19.852 ve 14.106 skorlarını aldım.
Güç tüketimi ise; masaüstünde işlemsiz beklemede ort 8-10 watt, YouTube vs izlerken ort 18-20 watt, oyunlarda da max 220 watt görünüyor. 650 watt SilverStone PSU ile kullanıyorum, sanırım gerçek değerlerde 550-600 watt kaliteli PSU’lar da yetecektir.
Fan sesine gelirsek; 60 dereceye kadar fanlar çalışmıyor, kartın sıcaklığına göre fan dönüş hızını kendi otomatik artıp-azalıyor. Fan dönüş hızında 2.000 rpm’e kadar kasa içi fanlarla yaklaşık aynı desibelde olduğundan fark edilebilir bir durum yok. 2.000 rpm’den sonra, özellikle 2.500 rpm civarında ben buradayım diyor. Oyunları kulaklık ile oynuyorsanız fan sesinin çok problem olacağını düşünmüyorum.
Kartın ısınması ve ısınmaya bağlı olarak artan fan dönüş hızını düşürmek için voltaj düşürme (undervolting) bir çözüm olabilir. MSI Afterburner ile kademe kademe test ederek stabil bir voltaj değeri bulabilirsiniz. Undervolting ile kartın voltajı düşük bir değere inince GPU’dan çektiği gücün değeri düşecek, düşen watt değerine bağlı olarak ısınma ve ısınmaya da bağlı olarak fan devir hızı düşecektir. Voltaj düşünce performans da düşer ama derseniz; şöyle söyleyeyim, uygun voltaj değerini bulunca %1-2 performans düşüşüne karşılık %10-15 arası sıcaklık ve fan devir hızı düşüşü alabiliyorsunuz. YouTube’da bununla ilgili birçok videoya ulaşabilirsiniz.
Genel olarak toparlarsak; bilgisayar kasası eski tip olup 3 fanlı modeller sığmıyorsa, 2024 yılında piyasa çıkmış orta-üst seviye bir NDIVIA ekran kartım olsun, 1080p ve özellikle 1440p’de güncel oyunları aksın diyorsanız, MSI kalitesinde ve amazon.com.tr güvencesiyle bu kartı tavsiye ederim. Ben memnum kaldım ve NVIDIA’nin driver konusunda stabilitesi düşünüldüğünde uzun yıllar bu kartını kullanırım diye düşünüyorum.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
First want to say if you've never owned an AMD reference gpu before, maybe you should learn a little more about it before you buy and ship it back. Yes it gets up to the low 80'c just like reference 1070's and 1080's. But many people are undervolting this gpu to keep the heat down and then in turn keep the fan noise down. The default fan profile, clock speeds and voltages can easily be adjusted.

Currently with flashed vega 64 bios, here are my settings in wattman
gpu frequency = -1.5% ~ 1607mhz max
voltage = 1.115v
mem frequency = 1025mhz
fan profile low = 700rpm
fan profile high = 3450rpm
card runs between 70c to 79c mostly staying around low 70's and mhz is usually 1530-1570 when being pushed. Yes the noise is a little loud but I wear headphones.

With those settings, it will tie an aftermarket gtx 1080 in timespy gpu scores of around 7,200 points.

Was lucky enough to snag this card for $399 previously, but see many cards are now dropping to $519 and $499, same with vega 64 dropping to $550ish. Please don't be stupid people and give 1 star for a product you don't own and are voting only based upon initial price and not upon actual market demands, we don't live in communism.

Amd cards and Ryzen cpu give the users more opportunity to adjust settings and tune to get more performance. It has plenty of more headroom for user improvements but require you to do some work or provide it aftermarket cooling. I would buy this again but wish game dev's could optimize their games more for vega. Most big name games run great, I usually get 90-160fps at 1440p on medium/high settings. Doom vulkan is a steady 110 to 160fps on ultra/nightmare 1440p with no AA. Great engine, need more programmers to jump onboard vulkan!!!

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Pros: Has given my AMD B550 Motherboard fast and reliable Thunderbolt connectivity. Have zero complaints about it once I got it working. It actually has been more reliable with my Thunderbolt 4 hub than a another PC with onboard support for Thunderbolt 4. I'm using dual DisplayPort pass-through to monitors running at 4K, with no issues. I have a bunch of USB devices connected through the hub including a 4K webcam, which also work with no issues. Everything connects and is functional from either cold boots or sleep and I've not had any issues with devices randomly disconnecting.

Contrary to other reviews, once this is set up correctly, I get the BIOS splash screen on monitors connected via a Thunderbolt hub and I'm able to use a keyboard/mouse connected through the hub before the OS boots.

Cons: The documentation provided with the card is woefully incomplete, so I'm here to get you up to speed.

Installation: The card requires an available PCI 4x slot, a dedicated Thunderbolt header on your motherboard, an available USB 2.0 header on your motherboard, and a six-pin PCIe connector from your power supply. Installing the card is as easy as connecting all of those things. Simply installing the card isn't enough, and this is where the documentation really fails. After installation, you will need to enter the PC's BIOS and enable Thunderbolt support. It is not enabled by default! This varies by motherboard, so it will involve searching all of the "advanced" settings. After you find the right settings, enable them, save settings, reboot. At that Windows should recognize the card and you can install the driver. One reboot later and Thunderbolt should be fully functional.

Which Thunderbolt port to use: The Thunderbolt ports on the card were clearly designed with daisy-chaining in mind and it impacts their functionality. Port 1 (the closest to the edge of the card) seems to be intended as the "Thunderbolt In" port. I wasn't able to get my hub to work with this port. Port 2 seems to be the "Thunderbolt Out" port. My hub works without issue when connected to the second port. Port 1 is powered, so it seems like you'd want to connect it to peripherals anyway, but again it's not explained in the documentation.

Other thoughts: My only other (minor) compliant is that the DisplayPort-in ports are DP1.4 and only support a single monitor per connection. There's two DP-ins, so it's not a big deal as long as you have two available DP connectors on your GPU.

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I'm using the ASUS Pro WS TRX50-SAGE motherboard with an AMD Ryzen Threadripper 7970x, 384GB of V-Color RAM (TR596G60D432Q), and a Silverstone XE360-TR5 cooler. This combination is working well and I'm very happy with it. I did, however, run into a few problems along the way...

1) I tried using a 140mm Noctua NH-U14S TR5-SP6 air cooler with this board, but it would not fit - the cooling fins interfered with the motherboard's cooling at the front (and maybe rear) of the board. A 92mm Noctua NH-D9 TR5-SP6 cooler does fit, but might not provide adequate cooling depending on the CPU being used.

2) Placing certain GPUs in the PCIe slot nearest to the CPU caused the 10Gb Lan port to not work. Moving the problematic card (Radeon PRO W6600) to another slot worked - unfortunately, due to other problems, it ended up in one of the PCIe Gen 4 slots instead of one of the PCIe Gen 5 slots.

3) When using multiple GPUs, boot messages and BIOS/EFI config are output using the GPU placed in the second PCIe slot from the CPU. For my particular use case, I'd have preferred to be able to set the slot used for this purpose. (I couldn't find a BIOS setting which did this.)

4) The board supports the use of two power supplies, but I used just one. When using one, in addition to the 24-pin ATX connector, it also requires two 8-pin CPU connections, one 8-pin PCIe power connection, and one 6-pin PCIe power connection. This may or may not be a problem depending on the power supply chosen. (I used a Seasonic Prime PX-1600.)

5) I failed to get the USB 20Gbps Type-C® Front Panel connector to work.

6) I ended with more fans than fan headers on the motherboard; I used Thermaltake fan hub to work around this problem.

7) The Q-CODE (diagnostic) LEDs will be hidden by a double slot card placed in PCIe slot #5.

8) There are three M.2 slots, but the maximum length is 80mm (used by 2280-sized M.2 devices). I have a 22100 Intel Optane device that I wanted to place in one of these slots.

9) Eight connectors (two PCIe power connectors), USB 5Gbps header, four SATA ports, and the SlimSAS port) are accessed from the front (as opposed to the top) of the board. This was probably done to provide clearance for long GPUs. It also make cable management cleaner, depending on the case being used. However, again depending on the case, it can be really hard to plug/unplug cables into/from these ports. That said, that section of the board is narrower, front-to-back, in order to make it easier to access these connectors. With the case that I used, once I installed the cooler, there was very little room to operate in the space available.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
This thing does exactly what it says. It just works. I Hooked it up to an old HP Prodesk 600 G2 mini. I Plugged the included oculink adapter to the mini pc’s m.2 slot and it fired right up without any issues. Before I tried the eGPU i made certain to update the mini pc’s bios and all the drivers. I also got all the windows 11 updates installed before starting. I used an older 500watt psu and a GTX-980 GPU with this eGPU dock. I Downloaded the GPU drivers and everything works flawlessly. Because the oculink adapter takes up the nvme m.2 slot you have to use the ata SSD connector for your storage needs.
People having connection issues using this eGPU dock/adapter are running into computers that are not compatible. Generally when it doesn’t work it is not the adapter/eGPU docks fault but that of the pc your connecting to. The other issue generally is that it’s not always easy to know if your mini/laptop etc is compatible with an eGPU. One way to find out is go to the iegpu website that shows many working configurations where adding an eGPU worked. There you can get help to resolve your issue if you’re having one. The key here is to do your research first to see if it’s viable before you start. This cannot be over stressed.
I ran GPU stress tests with FurMark on this older 4GB vram GPU. I got about 61-65 frames a second and in real world gaming tests using Borderlands 3s built in bench test with high settings I got on average of 61-63 fps at 1080p. Before I added this eGPU to the HP mini-pc the game would not run at all on the integrated UHD-630 graphics. I will be trying a GTX-Titan with 12GB of vram next to see how it performs. One other thing I should mention is that I installed Windows 11 pro on a mini pc that does not meet the hardware requirements for that install. This presented absolutely zero problems. Overall this dock is solid and works as advertised right out of the box with a pc that is compatible. I highly recommend this dock. I will be 3D printing a pc case for the whole setup next. The information is out there on how to ensure success when adding an external GPU using this dock or others like it.
If you have an older mini-pc or laptop with an available m.2 slot that is compatible and a spare psu and GPU then this could be an overall cheap setup to bring life to an old computer. I have included photos of the build. I hope this helps.

This performs great, especially if your dealing with an integrated GPU such as a mini PC. So why 4 stars? Well the GPU card don't fit all the way down into the PCIE Slot; as the plate that is affixed on the end of the card where your display ports are located bottoms out. So how to solve this problem?
A. (On GPU) Grind the tabs off a few millimeters.
B. (On E-GPU stand) Grind deeper slots to allow the tabs to pass thru.
C. Seat the card into the slot and use strong double sided tape to hold the PCIE Board in place. A small piece per corner where the screws normally go will be sufficient.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
The Flux Pro is hands down the best case I have ever personally come across in years of building PCs for myself, friends and family.
- Nicely shipped, comes in a box with molded foam padding holding the case securely in place.
- Includes plenty of screws etc. for various arrangements, multiple SSDs, as well as a nice transparent plastic screw case/organizer with movable separators.
- Spacious and easy to build in. Plenty of space for large CPU coolers and GPUs. Comfortably fits Noctua NH-D15 with room to spare.
- Great options for cable management inside the case with preinstalled loop straps for cable bundling. Existing cables inside the case (e.g. for front panel) are very well managed also.
- Included fans are very efficient and high quality, getting 6 of them included makes this case not only great quality but also a great value. They come pre-installed and hooked up to a small daughter board near the front/top panel with nicely routed cabling.
- Excellent and quiet air cooling performance. Using AMD 9800X3D and NH-D15 cooler, Sapphire AMD 7900XT GPU with default curves on the case fans, baseline 40% on the NH-D15 up to about 60C and an aggressive curve ramping quickly to 100% by 80C. The resulting system is totally silent for basic use and nearly all gaming loads; fans only become audible under very CPU heavy loads like code or shader compilation. Most of the time the GPU fan (and some GPU coil whine...) are the loudest thing in the system. I rarely ever see the CPU above about 65C, and even maxing out all cores I simply can't get it much above 76C with instant peak of 81-82C before fans catch up. Of course the 9800 and Noctua also get credit for this, but it's truly impressive how quiet it is.
- The HDD rack in the lower bay is easy to completely remove if you aren't using it, for slightly better airflow from the two lower fans pulling up through the bottom of the case.
- Power supply is easy to install with plenty of room for dealing with cables thanks to the large mostly empty lower bay.
- The mesh front panel and small holes on the bottom panel do a good job of minimizing dust in the case. Not perfect, but very good given the outstanding airflow of the case. The spacious interior also makes it easy to clean.
- The USB ports and power button on the top/front panel are solid and firmly mounted.
- The CPU/GPU temperature display works well (with required software installed) and is kind of cool.
- I didn't really care about the wood accent when I purchased, but it looks quite good and is a nice "premium" touch.
- No quality issues with my unit of any kind.

A small nit, but depending on the arrangement of your motherboard, the cables from the front panel may be very slightly on the short side. Not really a problem, but for one of the cables from the front panel I had to basically force a shortest path diagonally across the back of the motherboard (ignoring most cable management) to be able to reach the far left side of the bottom edge of the mobo.

This is without question the best case I've ever built a system in, after 25 years of building computers. Everything was thought out extremely well and everything has a purpose. The ventilation into the shroud area is present front, back and bottom, with reverse flow fans to draw some of that air up to the GPU. The top comes completely off for full access to placing fans, radiators, or even hooking things up through the top while installing components.

The top and rear have a sliding track that you can move your fans along to be in the location you want, and the whole 3 fan assembly up front has 5 different positions to move, up or down. I didn't have to use one zip tie and ended up with the best cable management I've ever had in probably 30 builds thanks to the multitude of perfectly located cutouts and the velcro cable tracks.

Included is a quality screw box with strong, good quality metal screws of all the types you will need to build your system. All are in labeled packets. I had no problem fitting any of my components in. Every piece has room and air around it and my system stays much cooler than it ever did with a 4070 Ti Super and a12900k. The case is rather heavy, so be aware of that before you lift your completed system. It is solid steel for the most part and I found very little if any flex, even with both sides and the top off.

1 TB Crucial M.2 Gen 4

Corsair 1000w PSU

As I needed additional powered USB headers I also added a Corsair Internal 4-Port USB 2.0 Hub - 4X 9-Pin USB 2.0 Ports for the Commander Core XT and Lian Li Controllers to function.
Thermal Grizzly Kryonaut Thermal Paste (removed the stock paste with AIO using TG cleaner wipes as well for better contact).
ThermalRight AMD5 CPU Shield - This allows the AIO or Waterblock (if doing a custom loop) to make WAY better contact with the CPU HS. It can be a little nerve wracking as your removing the cpu mount and installing this one but its worth it. As the AM5 CPU has no pins (the mobo now has the pins), its imperative you are gentle on the placement. Best way I found to install this shield was to place the CPU into the socket, then remove the cpu holder so this way you can't damage the cpu or pins as they are socketed. Installing the shield from that point is easy, just don't overtighten it. Theres a bunch of youtube videos on this process. Definitely recommend reviewing them before attempting this step.

I upgraded from my old Ryzen 5 2600X system with a GTX 960 SSC 4GB card and a 512gb M.2 Gen 2 drive.

Needless to say this was quite the upgrade from my old system.
Cinebench scores on my 2600X even with a mild overclock was only around 7200.

After getting everything configured/setup and Windows 11 Pro installed with all updates and enabling EXPO1 (RAM OC) and enabling SAM in the BIOS I started my benchmarking.

Cinebench score with just EXPO1 enabled baseline was 28745. What a jump!
CPU temp on the multi-core threading with the 360 AIO only went as high as 82c (AMD rates these to run at 95c as normal operating temp so it was well below even that).
Haven't done any OC'ing other than enabling EXPO1 yet since I really don't need to as the CPU and GPU run everything maxed out.

Tested on a few games on max/ultra settings and below are what I got FPS wise:

The Division 2 (All settings maxed and on DX12) - Avg 125fps on 3440 x 1440 165hz resolution
Aliens: Fireteam Elite - Avg 160fps on 3440 x 1440 165hz resolution
Borderlands 2 (older game I know but love to play it with max settings) - Avg 476fps on 3440 x 1440 165hz resolution
Forza Horizon 5 - Ultra Settings (max) including Ray Tracing - Avg 155fps on 3440 x 1440 165hz resolution
Aliens: Colonial Marines (older game) - Avg 190FPS on 3440 x 1440 165hz resolution
Warframe - Avg 155fps on 3440 x 1440 165hz resolution

Pairing this CPU and GPU together worked great and the CPU itself is a beast. It does get hot when it turbo's up into the 5ghz range which is why you need a really good cooler (either AIO or custom loop) to keep the temps in check.

If you do that, this CPU will be everything you need and then some.

One thing I always tell people is to take your time, plan out your PC parts you want for what you want the system to do (video editing, gaming, streaming, etc). Don't be afraid to look around for good deals. I scored the AIO Cooler off Newegg for a much cheaper price than Amazon had it and it works beautifully and the LCD screen is just a nice "geek" factor to put JPG's or GIF's there.

Once you have everything, take your time when building it. You may run into an issue here or there which is normal. First boot on AM5 systems is sometimes slow (Memory has to train) and you may see it cycle on/off for up to 1 minute. Mine did this and on the 4th power cycle it posted and I could get into the BIOS and everything showed up correctly.

Good luck enthusiasts and hope this review helped with anyone looking at this CPU for their system!
Its worth it!

text:
*** EDIT ***
I have achieved eGPU stability. Been training an AI model now for 8+ hours with no disconnect. No scientific method here so these last changes could be the only ones needed:

NVIDIA App / Graphics / Global Settings / Power Management Mode / Prefer maximum performance
Windows 11 Power Options / High performance vs. Balanced (Default)
Windows 11 Power Options / Turn off the display / Plugged in / Never

Also, I had some intermittent disconnects when running the laptop hard. I was powering the laptop off the Breakaway as it's rated to deliver 240W. Put the laptop brick back into the "designated" laptop thunderbolt port and the disconnects went away. So no laptop power from the Breakaway (USB-C sorts it all out?) improved things.
*** EDIT ***

My experience is with the 850 Box, an RTX 5070 Ti GPU, and a new AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX laptop. The GPU takes up to 300W under full load. The Sonnet Breakaway Box is rated at 850W and the internal RTX power cable has a 600W tag on it (other 250W on the other standard looking cables, I imagine?). I'm only using the 850 Box for the GPU running AI and powering the laptop through the provided Thunderbolt cable. Not using the other features on the Breakaway Box (no wired network) or the GPU (no displays). In summary, the external cabling is the included power cable and the included Thunderbolt cable to the laptop. Only internal cable used is the one for the RTX.

Thunderbolt "is" USB so reverence has to be paid to Windows as it likes to turn off idle USB devices and cycle the GPU connection:

In Device Manager / Universal Serial Bus devices / * / Power Management / Allow the computer to turn off this device... / Uncheck the box
In Settings / Bluetooth & devices / USB / USB battery saver / Slide to "Off"

I found multi-media web pages would also like to cycle the GPU off and on so:

In Device Manager / Sound, video and game controllers / NVIDIA *Audio* / Disable
In Settings / System / Display / Graphics / Optimization for windowed games / Slide to "Off"
In Settings / System / Display / Graphics / Advanced graphics settings / Hardware-accelerated GPU scheduling / Slide to "Off"
In Settings / System / Display / Graphics / Advanced graphics settings / Variable refresh rate / Slide to "Off"
Verify for all apps in Settings / System / Display / Graphics / <App> / GPU preference / Let Window decide (Power saving) -- don't do anything special
Verify for all apps in Settings / System / Display / Graphics / <App> / Optimization for windowed games / Off

And, reinstall ONLY the minimum amount of NVIDIA:

NVIDIA App 11.0.5...
NVIDIA CUDA Toolkit 13.1
NVIDIA Graphics Driver 576.88
NVIDIA FrameView SDK 1.5.11504...
***** NO NVIDIA HD Audio driver *****

This setup has been pretty stable with Windows 11 and Ubuntu on WSL2 both running AI models on the RTX 5070 Ti.

On Ubuntu, I did add the following to my C:\Users\%USERNAME%\.wslconfig file:

[general]
instanceIdleTimeout=-1

[wsl2]
vmIdleTimeout=-1

Don't let all this extra configuration dissuade you. It's a lovely box and well worth the effort.

DisplayLink drivers are required and Windows did not automatically detect/install for me; WAVLINK includes a link to the drivers in the box. Drivers are included for Windows, MacOS, Ubuntu (specifically), and, for some reason, Android; I'm eager to see the Android tablet with PCIe 4x ports. Once installed, there is no fuss; it just works, at least on Windows 11.

This card DOES support at least 100hz output on 1080p, but I'm not sure exactly what the limits are with varying numbers of monitors connected; there is not much in the way of documentation beyond the URL that you aren't seeing in the listing. In theory, the DL7400 chip itself supports 10k@60hz and four 4k monitors at 120hz, but the maximum specs of the chip are not necessarily the maximum specs of the card, and the documentation says nothing beyond "4k@60hz." It will likely take me a fair amount of waiting for a 10k monitor to show up on Vine to test with this :) It may alternately be more of a thermal limit; we're left to guess.

While this version of the card has 4 HDMI ports, WAVLINK does offer other configurations including a 2 HDMI, 2 DisplayPort variant. Heat output while the card is running seems fairly low (no problem touching it, not much warmer than my hand), but I am not running 4x4k.

Edit: I ran into issues where Desktop Window Manager on Windows 11 began consuming upwards of 50GB of RAM while using this, eventually crashing the system. The solution was to update graphic drivers, specifically the integrated Intel graphics drivers.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Let me preface this whole things by saying that Kryonaut is a really good thermal paste for cpus. It helped decrease my tdie temps by a massive margin (over 5 degrees), and thermal conductivity is impressive while being easy to apply. But putting it on gpus... let's just say I bought this before I had actually done proper research because I had heard so much good about it. *sigh* time for the long boring essay...

**TL;DR: pump out is bad for long term thermals and this has especially bad pump out. anything with IHS (cpu) gooood, anything without (delidded cpu, gpu, socs, laptops, etc.) baaad

A lot of people tend to think thermal paste is either all the same or only look at conductivity. However, with this paste, I figured out the hard way that thermal paste is way more than heat dissapation. Pump out occurs through many repeated cycles of rapid heating and cooling and causes the thermal paste to dissipate outwards and leave little to no paste on the core, usually through a long time period (3-10 years, depending on quality). This is more prominent on gpus as those have no ihs and tend to heat and cool more violently than cpus do. Thicker, more viscous thermal pastes are less prone to this. Unfortunately, this thermal paste in particular has especially terrible pump out because it's thin and watery.
It worked WONDERS on my cpu as I mentioned earlier. An already great temp of 65c or so fell to 55-60 while gaming in ambient 22-27c. No pump out issues and it stayed like this until I changed coolers.
On my gpu, it worked well - at first. 55c with 8 degree delta between hot spot and core. It almost instantly (within a month or two) started to have bad deltas (meaning pump out was causing die to heat up in certain spots more than others). Delta was around 8c, then slowly rose to 15c+ (worst I saw was 20c) and core temp also rose from 55c to 60c to 65c. When I replaced it with a thicker, much more resiliant thermal paste (thermalright tfx), it has been consistently good at ~57-61c and 10-12c delta for the past 3 months.

All in all, it's a great paste that has amazing thermal conductivity (although that standard is nonexistent). your cpu temps will drop if you are replacing old or otherwise low quality thermal paste. However, it's a lot of money for the amount of paste you get, and being the way it is, it is not designed for direct die contact, so bear that in mind. Be aware that different thermal pastes have different use cases, and this is not for gpus. If you want that from thermal grizzly, there is hydronaut and liquid metal (though I have not used either). I personally just recommend arctic mx5 and tfx and maybe noctua nt-h2.

Unlike many PSUs in the 1000+ watt range, this one maintains the small form factor of lower-powered PSUs, and it does so without getting overheated. Granted, I'm running an i7-13700k with my trust old GTX 1080ti, but still. One of the other major selling points of this PSU is that it has a dedicated 12V rail for your GPU. I have no issue running my old 1080ti on it and now I'm future-proofed for an eventual upgrade to an RTX 4090. Full modularity is always great, of course, and this PSU comes with plenty of cables for every type of connection you might need (except IDE, but you're spending way too much on a PSU if you're using this for a retro PC, lol).

Also, I know some reviews of this PSU say that can get a little noisy under heavy loads, but I've yet to experience that. However, that could also be because I'm already running a huge air-cooling setup and can't hear the PSU's fan. Having a whisper-quiet PC has never been a concern for me, anyway. I will say, it would be nice if MSI had used a 140mm fan rather than a 120mm, as the chassis of this PSU certainly could accommodate it. A minor design criticism, ultimately. My only other criticism is that with a bottom-mounted, fan-down installation, there's a big information sticker that's highly visible on the face-up side. This doesn't affect anything, it just looks ugly. I don't know where else you'd put such a sticker, though, given that there's minimal real estate for one, but you'd think that as a gaming-oriented PC hardware manufacturer, MSI would've considered that many gamers care almost as much about aesthetics in their builds as they do performance.

As far as PSU's go, it's a nice-looking box, other than that damn sticker. I certainly wouldn't pass on this PSU for that, though. This thing is a beast and a great choice, despite being on the pricey end, that will future-proof your system. Also, that sticker could relatively easily be removed if you so chose to do so. Overall, 5/5, highly recommended.

My laptop (Vector 16 HX AI) sports two Thunderbolt 5 ports, so this was a welcome upgrade!

It's a bit pricey when it doesn't even include a power supply, but I had been waiting forever for this upgrade.

I feel the TB5 interface has less glitchy oddities than the TB4 eGPU, too. TB5 seems like a more solid connection in addition to better performance.

まず、本体（筐体）の感想は以下の通り。
・GPU差しづらい。3スロット厚だと端子部分はめ込む位置見え難くて怖かった
・ケースをはめ直す際に四隅のレールに綺麗に嵌らないことが多く、作りが粗い気が…
・高負荷中の発熱はケース上部とファン側（右サイド）が強め
・筐体は冷えるのが思ったより早くて良い。低負荷に戻って数分もすれば温度が落ち着く

接続についてはThunderbolt4/5ないしUSB4で接続すれば即使える、と謳ってはいますが
組み込んだGPUに対応するドライバのインストールは別途必要でしたのでご注意を。
ちなみに初回接続時にRazor Synapseのインストール案内が出ますが必須では無いです。

また、自環境では接続先PCに他の50シリーズのGPUとドライバが存在する影響か
PC起動後に接続すると異常終了することがありましたので、
似た環境の方は試した上で起動前に接続しておいたほうが無難かも知れません。

性能について以下環境のThunderbolt5接続で特に設定を弄らずに使用した結果ですが
3DMarkTimeSpyのベンチマークスコアで「30843」（添付画面）。
仮にデスクトップで出せる最高性能がスコア「47487」だとすると結果は約65％、
某BTOの5090デスクトップの最大スコア「約37000」と比較すると約83%となり、
期待していたのですが結局ThunderBolt5でも良くて８割、または７割弱の性能しか出てないようです。
勿論CPUや電源などがボトルネックになっている可能性が考えられますが、現状確認できる限りでは結果の通り。
今のところゲームやAI生成など数日試した限り、動作に問題は起きていません。

＜検証環境＞
端末CPU ：Core Ultra9 275HX（Thunderbolt5対応ノートPC）
組込電源 ：850W（CORSAIR RM850x）
組込GPU ：RTX5090（ZOTAC SOLID OC）

まとめると、性能は本来の７〜８掛け程度で見ておいたほうが良いものの
Thunderbolt/USB4接続可能で現行環境より性能向上が見込めそうであれば
十分に検討の価値はある製品だと思います。
本体端末と別筐体である関係上、CPU等との熱干渉も避けられるのでデスクトップ環境よりGPUのパーツ寿命の伸びが期待出来るかも知れません。
ただ、性能減を考慮すると出来るだけ上位のGPUが欲しいところで
本製品と併せてどうしてもお高い買い物になる為、割高に感じるし、ご時勢的にも悩ましいところ。

なお、どのように電源やGPUを組み込んで使うかの手順は
解説されているサイト様がありましたので商品名で探すと良いかと思います。

I took a chance on this item in an effort to use the Samsung 960 PRO Series - 2TB PCIe on my iMac Pro. The adapter I used was the Ableconn PEXM2-SSD M.2 NGFF PCIe SSD to PCI Express 3.0 x 4 Host Adapter Card. I went with a non-StarTech adapter because at the time of purchase this was one seemed to be rated better by Amazon users. My goal was to achieve same, near or faster read/write speeds than the internal storage on my iMac Pro. The good news is, the StarTech Thunderbolt chassis connected immediately. I gave this 4 stars simply for the fact that it worked. I was very apprehensive as there were literally no other reviews. But I assure you it does work. I ended up not keeping this item because I could not achieve anywhere near listed speeds for the SSD. Listed speed for write/read on the Amazon page is 2100/3500. But I achieved 950/2300 respectively. I don't think this was the fault of the StarTech item, but I can't say for certain. My guess is it was a combination of the adapter and slower thunderbolt cable. If your situation was anything like mine (buying Apple) and you're looking at this as a cheaper solution to expanding storage, my suggestion is bite the bullet and just go for bigger internal storage. If you're looking at this for connecting other components such as a video card, I think chances are strong it will function.

Edit: I forgot to mention that this comes with a fairly short thunderbolt cable and you'll probably want to purchase a longer one. Also it comes with power plugs for both U.S. and Europe.

Edit 2: I managed to raid together 2 Samsung X5 m.2. The raid speed of these drives greatly outdoes my iMac Pro’s internal read/write speed. Just make sure your drives are connected to separate buses.

text:
It took a bit to get the GPU dock. Amazon lost or damaged, who knows, my first order. After 9 days Amazon threw in the towel and said it was undeliveable and gave
me a refund. Ordered again and the it showed up 2 days later.

The new unit runs as expected. It is quiet. I read complaints about power supply fan noise but in mine it is barely audible. There are few things you should know, most of which is covered by others in the comments and Reddit.

1. There is no on/off switch, the power supply and fan will remain on continously if the dock has power. Based on other user feedback, I installed a switch found here: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B07QJWLZFJ?ref=ppx_yo2ov_dt_b_fed_asin_title (to easily turn the unit off when not in use).
2. Depending on your computer CPU and OS (I have the Geekom A6 running Windows 11 pro) you will likely need to optimize your settings and cable configuration to get the full benefit and smooth usage of the eGPU. The Geekon A6 has some power saving priorities buit in that I had to turn off as well. I'm a retired old fart and got it figured out with a helping hand from Chrome AI. The AI pulls much of its advice and summarizes easy to follow instructions from Reddit users and Youtobe tutorials. I found it easier to use Chrome AI and work through my questions and fixes than searching the internet. Worked for me.
3. For now I have my integrated graphics turned off and everything runs through the eGPU. You will likely need to modify some setting in your programs, clear some cache, etc to get everything running smoothly. I'm not a power user, the GPU is a ASUS Strix 1070 Ti with 8GB and games (Cyber punk 2077, Mad Max,etc.) run on my 75Hz monitor smoothly at or near 75 FPS.

Once you install it, do your research, and set it up so it is optimized for your system, I think you'll be satisfied with performance. Just remember, no hot swapping available when using Occulink (I use USB4).

If I had to do it all over (I was too impatient to wait longer for delivery), I would probably get the Aoostar EG03 which has dual USB4/TB5 ports (80 Gbps bandwidth vs 40Gbps on Aoostar EG02) alongside OCuLink connectivity which would better future proof it if I decide to upgrade my GPU and mini PC.

Edit: It died on day 28, thankfully within return, no hassle, timeframe. Ordered a replacement, see how it works out.

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
The herculx by Asus ROG is a cool, helpful, but ridiculous product.

It's very useful for propping up these massive new RTX 30 series and later cards, which I just bought for myself after using a gtx 1000 series for many years. Though for me this was very much optional as I have an Asus ROG Strix motherboard which has reinforced anti-sag PCIe ports. However I like to baby my electronics, so I got this anyways.

If you're like me and you are a big gamer, and love all the fancy RGB stuff, and gaming knick-knacks, then you'll love this. If you also don't have a reinforced motherboard, you'll definitely need this as the RTX 30 series are huge cards, they feel like something that belongs in a vehicle engine rather than a PC part.

The herculx is a very well engineered device. It has a small little "foot" on it which can be dialed to adjust the height down to the millimeter. It's got a push-button that allows you to manually adjust the height in bigger volumes so you don't have to sit there and turn the dial forever, it fits a wide variety of spaces so it should work with most cases/PC setups, however keep in mind your measurements and spacing just in case.

I call the herculx ridiculous because it's so over the top, it's got RGB lighting of course which plugs into an addressable RGB header on your motherboard, and can be setup just like any other RGB peripheral device. The colors are also very vibrant and the device has this "holographic" look to it which is really cool.

This thing also has a detachable, magnetic level that fits right on it for storage which is another reason I call it ridiculous, however it is still very useful if you're paranoid about your card sagging.

The one down side to a GPU stand like this is that GPUs aren't exactly designed for stands. I say that because GPUs tend to have a lot of fans, and you have to be careful not to place the stand touching one of these fans or you may damage your GPU. In fact I bought a ROG Strix brand RTX 30 series card and I found very little spaces for the stand's little "foot" to sit under, I had to place it in a tiny little space along the edge of the card between two of the fans in order for it to hold the card, but also be out of the way.

TL;DR This is a great item, and it'll hold a GPU up for sure, it's well engineered and is very smooth operating, it has RGB via an addressable header plug (3 prong) and even comes with a magnetic, detachable level. It's got a cool holographic style face to it which makes the lighting look super cool. And lastly it is covered in ROG branding so you can show off your ROG dedication.

I wouldn't recommend this to just anyone, however I WOULD 100% recommend this to someone who has the money for it, and needs to prop up their GPU to prevent sagging/damage to their motherboard. It's a great product and though at the time of me buying this it was $40USD, I would probably buy it again, there are cheaper GPU stands out there, but this one is so well made it just screams quality. Even the packaging was incredible.

text:
A picture speaks a thousand words.

Amazon in their infinite wisdom decided that the best method to ship a product that must remain watertight lest it destroy the $2200+ video card it has been bolted to would be to just slap a shipping label on it and ration out some prime tape. In the same order far less valuable things that were far less fragile were packed in a shipping box.

As can happen with them the thermal pads, especially the 0.5mm thick ones on the unit I received had gone stiff as dry play-doh. Thermal pads can come in many different flavors and much like thermal compound can cure, dry up, become useless. These had and the ride didn't help. Amazon being Amazon sought to fix it by replacing it, it being the entire waterblock. Really green thinking from Amazon there.

Reaching out to Corsair was fun. CorsairArt was quick to check with the Hydro X team to see if thermal pads were offered as a part. They are not. I had not heard back from Corsair on my ticket which wasn't surprising so I went ahead and ordered replacement pads and paste. Finally a response from Corsair that they would inquire about thermal pads. I informed them CorsairArt already checked into that. They then offered to send out another waterblock if I sent them this one for their engineering team to study.

I declined, just cover the cost of the thermal pads and compound. Surely Corsairs engineers have unraveled the mystery of thermal pads. That was that, Corsair gave that as the only option. Send multiple heavy chunks of copper on an intercontinental tour and pretend like Canada isn't experiencing hellish droughts and some of the warmest winters in our lives. Reimbursing the pittance for the thermal pads I purchased is somehow better for the world in general in this scenario.

Do yourself a world of good and support a different brand.

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
The install isn't straightforward, and the manual doesn't help.

First, separate the two large pieces by unscrewing the silver thumbscrew.

Then, use the included screws to fasten the PCI-E slot onto the mount, there are 2 standoffs for that purpose. Screw down the graphics card's slot blend with 2 of the screws that came with the product.

Now install the backplate that screws to the case, using two screws that came with your case. Those will fit better than what's included with this product.

Now install your graphics card on the slot on the bracket, and then plug the PCI-E connector into your motherboard. Make absolutely certain that on both ends, the connectors fully engage and that the little peg and the end of each slot engages (the "lock" to ensure the card doesn't slide out.)

Finalize the install. It's not a very difficult install but if you try to do this all in the case with the product fully assembled, you're going to have a hard time.

After all is said and done, the bracket works very well. I am showing it in a Fractal North XL. Zero problems with the PCI-E extender, all benchmarks and tests work exactly as without. It's a very good product for the price but I am deducting a point for lack of better instructions.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I was extremely lucky to stumble upon this case while looking for a Mini-ITX. It's made of durable, good quality metal that's heavy (but not too heavy), small with a lot of room, and extremely versatile (just about every panel of this thing comes off without any tools - just need a screwdriver for the top and bottom panels). It's pretty much perfect for both experts and first-time builders who want a smaller compact PC.

This was my very first time building my own PC, and despite it being inside such a small case, the NR200 made it extremely easy to install. There are tons of places for cable management ties with unlimited potentional for different layouts. The case also has so much airflow that it cools the case extremely well. You also can't beat the price either - it's comparable to a Ncase M1 (but slightly bigger) while being less than half the cost.

There are only a couple issues that I ran into:

- The backside of the case does not have a lot of room to run cables. Not a deal breaker (it was still very doable) but you'll need to strap down the cables on the backside as well in order to get the panel to shut. If it had just another half inch it would be perfect.

- There are many mixed answers on this, but the version without the riser does NOT come with a glass side panel (or at least mine didn't). If you want a see-through side panel, you'll have to opt for the PCI riser version.

Overall I'm extremely happy with this case, it made my first build in a Mini-ITX case very easy. My PC runs very cool and there's lots of room for expansion once the 20 & 30 series cards drop in price again.

My build:
- AMD Ryzen 5 3600
- GeForce GTX 1050 Ti 4GB
- Team T-Force Vulcan TUF 16GB 3200MHz
- 512GB M.2 NVMe Boot Drive w/ 2 500GB 2.5 SSDs
- Gigabyte B550I Aorus Pro AX MOBO
- Corsair SF 450 Watt PSU
- 3 x 120mm PWM Fans

text:
The TLDR is that this case is great. I bought another to build a new work computer, and both cases are keeping cool. I did replace the fans with Scythe 140mm fans on the radiator and 120mm slim fans for the bottom on both my home and work builds since both are similar enough.

It's been a while since I built a computer and kind of set it and forgot about it. I've dusted out the home machine once since I got that one. Otherwise my only gripe was the paint on the original case but again, that literally buffed out. The second case didn't even have much in the way of spots on the paint or anything.
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Original review below:

I had an original nr200 that I moved an old itx build into about a year ago and loved it. I honestly wish I had kept it instead of selling and keeping my atx build. But I probably wouldn't have gone with this then. So, it's a win. After waiting 7+ months for this case, between seeing it in reviews and not knowing where to get it until it hit Amazon/Newegg, I'd say it was worth the wait.

This comes with two minor caveats, for me at least, that I can't imagine many people have run into.

I got my *first* delivery and was missing the riser cable and one of the pcie power cables. The box looked unopened so I'll say it was a packing issue from the factory. I did try to just go through the order page to exchange it but was only given the option to return. I'd imagine this is due to the cost of the item as a whole. A call with an Amazon rep got this turned into an exchange.

The second little gripe I have is with the paint. On the first and second item, the paint looked a little weird. Not really scuffs but I had to take a little polish to the panels to clean them up. Not a big deal, but if someone is paying close to or over 450 for this great package, and technically for a specific color, I would think the qc on the paint would be a better.

I popped an x570i Strix board with my 5900x and Strix 3080. Everything fit like a glove. The cooler does have a little whine in the pump but I keep the machine of to the side and have a fan on most of the time so it's not audible. I did change the top fans out though for the Silverstone Penatrator ARGB fans to get a little more flair but the stock fans were more than capable of get the hot air through the radiator. I matched these up with their 120mm Slimmer fans.

If you don't already have a computer built or want to downsize from an ATX build like my situation, this is the way to go. Be weary that the psu comes with 2x PCIE power cables that have 2 plugs daisy chained each. I don't really see this as a problem but I know there are disadvantages to this according to the internet pc building gods. I had a custom cable made anyway to add a third and there are plenty of people on etsy that can provide such a product or a full set of cables if needed. I paired this with a set of those 90 degree adapters too so it looks extra clean.

I think if Coolermaster sold this version of the case, without the psu, cooler, riser, etc, for the same price as the normal nr200, I think they'd still sell a ton. Great case overall, probably never going mid/full size build again because of it.

text:
En un mercado tan minoritario y poco explorado como lo es el de las computadoras de alta gama en bajos volúmenes de espacio, es muy agradable encontrar sorpresas de este tamaño.
Si bien el gabinete NR200 y el NR200 MAX no fueron nuevos en el mercado, la version NR200P MAX viene a corregir algunas cosas algo molestas de la versión anterior a cambio de cerrar las opciones de montura de la GPU y de colocación de enfriamiento de CPU.

Empecemos hablando de su lógica y bien planteada idea de flujo de aire, aquí nos dan preinstalado un enfriador líquido de alta gama con 2 ventiladores enormes que sirven de salida de aire caliente. Mucha gente tiende a decir que esto es un error. Pero pueden ver qué en realidad las cosas de mantienen a una temperatura muy buena en general.

Todo viene preinstalado y colocado de forma lógica y tranquila para la construcción. Prueba de ello es que la fuente de 850 watts tiene cables completamente personalizados, con una longitud medida a milímetros para quedar perfecto en el 99% de placas base Mini ITX del mercado.

Su sistema de montura de discos 2.5 es sin herramientas y perfectamente seguro, sumado a ello, los cortes de la parte posterior del gabinete son todos brillantes y muy bien colocados. He podido reinstalar un SSD sin dolor, sin desarmar nada, solo sacando la tapa posterior del gabinete, sin ningún problema.

Hablando de las tapas, nos incluyen una hermosa de cristal templado y todas, absolutamente todas, se pueden quitar sin necesidad de hacer uso de ninguna clase de herramienta. Las tapas con agujeros de respiración son ambas idénticas, quitando problemas de confusión y te brindan además guías puestas incluso en el mismo gabinete para saber qué movimientos debes realizar para su instalación y su remoción.

La bomba de agua es sorpresivamente más silenciosa de lo que yo creía y bajo carga muy estresante mi GPU bajo en promedio 15 grados de temperatura de lo que tenía previamente, en mi gabinete RVZ02.

Por esta razón, le doy 5 estrellas, porque veo a mucha gente seleccionando este gabinete para quedarse con el durante varias actualizaciones de GPU y CPU (En especial para AMD, ya que es compatible con AM5).

Recomendaciones;
1.- Recomiendo verificar la compatibilidad de la GPU con el gabinete previo a la compra. No me mal entiendan, se puede incrustar el 98% de las cosas porque sacrificando un poco la altura del gabinete y la posibilidad de colocar el GPU "acostado", este gabinete nos permite montar cualquier GPU con PCI 4.0 en el. El problema es que algunos ensambladores de gráficas están llegando al absurdo de poner tarjetas que requieren hasta 4,5 slots, lo cual además de innecesario y ridículo, evitaría que ustedes puedan colocar este gabinete en su setup.

2.- Verifiquen la compatibilidad con Intel.
En serio... Gracias Intel, no sabes cómo amamos que cada nueva generación cambies a propósito el socket de enfriamiento para las CPU.
El gabinete viene con 4 sockets diferentes para Intel, y soy el primero en saber que no es suficiente. Verifiquenlo.
(GRACIAS AMD por hacer el socket AM5 compatible con todo AM4)

Puntos a mejorar;
1.- Precio.
No me mal entiendan, es un paquete 5 estrellas porque las piezas están 100% personalizadas para esta implementación. PERO, en ofertas puedes comprar sin problemas; 1.- NR200P, 2.- Fuente SFX de 850 watts, 3.- Enfriador de alta gama de 2 ventiladores en el radiador... Y todo eso te puede salir entre 50 a 100 dólares más barato de lo que tenemos aquí.
Si, vas a tener que lidiar con algunas cosas molestas de la versión anterior del gabinete, como la altura extra o cosas como que la colocación de la fuente es muy cercana a la motherboard y por tanto tendrás que pelear mucho con los cables de longitud estándar. Así que... Cae en ustedes si el tener más comodidad justifica el precio extra.

2.- Color.
Alguien más sabio que yo dijo una vez; "Puedes pedir el color que quieras, mientras sea negro."
Y aquí no existe esa opción (detalle muy menor)

Veredicto final.
Este es el paraíso de construcción Mini-ITX. De calle.
¿Es tu primera construcción de PC en tu vida o es tu primer PC Mini-ITX? Felicidades, no busques más.
Este gabinete tiene absolutamente todos los argumentos para convertirse en el favorito de absolutamente todos los constructores de este tamaño entusiasta.

Si bien, se le pueden señalar cosas como que es algo grande con sus 11 litros en volumen, Cooler Máster sabe aprovechar cada centímetro cúbico disponible para permitirnos tener seguridad en nuestra construcción y en nuestras temperaturas.

Tiene 5 estrellas por ser un producto excesivamente completo, a pesar de su precio que puede ser considerado premium.

I didn't fill up all of the fan spots as that would be too much, but low key wonder if that would leave some dead air space in the case. I did have a small issue with drive temps at the bottom bay since the only fans were towards the back acting as an exhaust and I don't want hot air to exhaust through the front. I was able to quickly 3D print a mod to the front of the case, just behind the wood veneer, to add 2 more 140 mm fans to intake air which worked perfectly, averaging 35 C on my 5 drives.

Given that I was only installing an ITX, I had zero issues with accessibility in a large case like this and cable management was absolutely no problem. The hard drive compartment require grommets to be installed on the hard drive to "slide" into the case with just a rubber handle to pull it out, it works but not the most elegant solution. The backplane was a bit sketch at first but proved to be good and reliable as it accepted the my drives with little issues and felt quite solid when pushing the drives into it.

All in all, great next step in a home NAS solution upgrading from my 3D printed NAS case with 2 drives and plenty of room for upgrades for performance and storage. Price was quite competitive with other NAS cases I was looking at but this looks much better in the living room than a tower. Worth it for an upgrade to a personal home server.

Pros:

Cons:
* The opening below/beside a fitted ATX motherboard's CPU power connectors, was too obscured/small to allow the PSU plug end of the cable to that connector to pass, so routing of it had to start without the motherboard screwed down.
* The supplied 1 above and 2 below, 3-pin 120mm fans are noticeably louder than my installed and running 11 8TB WD Red Pros [2] as RAIDZ3 [3]. I ordered a set of five quality 4-pin PWM fans, which can be chained, to replace them and hopefully improve this. No, fans don't always have to run full-blast all the time, and PWM allows motherboard or controller speed tuning.

text:
I picked up this Arctic MX‑4 thermal paste because I ran out of paste on my current CPU and wanted something high quality to get my temperatures back down and make sure my cooler was properly seated. I do a lot of PC building for gaming, content creation, and occasional 3D work, so good thermal management is important to me.

Even though it’s sitting in my PC parts bag right now waiting for my next re-paste, Arctic MX‑4 has a strong reputation in the enthusiast community as one of the go‑to thermal compounds for everyday builds. It’s composed of carbon microparticles designed to fill microscopic gaps between the CPU and cooler to improve heat transfer more efficiently than stock paste or cheap alternatives.

In my system before I retired it, my CPU temps under load were around 55–60 °C, with idle temps around 38–42 °C—and that was with strong airflow around the cooler and stock paste that had seen better days. Based on typical results people get with MX‑4, switching to this paste often results in a noticeable drop in temps, around 3–5 °C, versus older or stock thermal compounds, which matches what many builders report when they upgrade.

One of the things I like about MX‑4 is that it’s non‑electrically conductive, so there’s no risk of shorting anything while applying it. It’s also known for long‑term stability, Arctic advertises years of performance without needing to reapply, which gives me confidence that once I put it on, it’ll stay effective through several builds or CPU cooler swaps.

Application was easy with the included spatula, and I appreciate that it’s a trusted, tried‑and‑true paste that many builders still use instead of stock stuff. If you’re upgrading your cooler or just need to refresh your TIM, this is a solid, affordable pick that’ll help keep temps in check without being overkill.

Ich habe das NZXT Vertical GPU Mounting Kit (AB-RH175-B1, 175 mm PCIe 4.0 x16) für meinen Build gekauft, um meine Grafikkarte optisch stärker in Szene zu setzen. Bereits beim Auspacken fällt die hochwertige Verarbeitung auf: Das Kit wirkt stabil, massiv und insgesamt sehr sauber gefertigt.

In meinem NZXT H6 Flow hat das Mounting Kit perfekt gepasst – wirklich wie angegossen. Die Montage lief völlig unkompliziert, alles sitzt stramm und sicher, und auch mit meiner GeForce RTX 5070 Ti gab es keinerlei Platz- oder Kompatibilitätsprobleme. Mechanisch und optisch harmoniert das Kit einfach hervorragend mit dem Gehäuse.

Das Kit macht einen sehr stabilen Eindruck, ohne wackelige Stellen oder Spiel. Das PCIe-4.0-Kabel hat genau die richtige Länge und setzt weder den Slot noch die GPU unter Spannung. Elektrisch läuft alles einwandfrei – keinerlei Leistungsverlust im Vergleich zur horizontalen Montage.

Auch die Optik stimmt: Der dezente, unauffällige Rahmen unter der GPU wirkt deutlich eleganter als viele andere Vertikal-Kits. Der Abstand zur Gehäusewand ist gut gewählt; nah für einen sauberen Look, aber weit genug, damit die Temperaturen der GPU absolut stabil bleiben.

Tipp:
Unbedingt im BIOS prüfen, ob der PCIe-Slot wirklich auf GEN 4 eingestellt ist. Manche Boards setzen diesen Wert automatisch auf GEN 3, was tatsächlich zu Leistungseinbußen führen kann. Ein kurzer Blick ins BIOS verhindert genau das.

Fazit:
Ein hochwertiges, stabiles und optisch sehr starkes Vertical-Mounting-Kit. Die Verarbeitung ist top, die Montage einfach, und besonders in NZXT-Gehäusen – wie meinem H6 Flow – passt alles perfekt zusammen. Wer seine Grafikkarte vertikal präsentieren möchte, bekommt hier ein absolut empfehlenswertes Produkt.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I love this case. Everything about it is a showpiece, so it's meant to be on full display on a desk or other sturdy surface. Don't hide this beauty under your desk or off in a corner! If you have a lot of RGB elements, they will really shine in this case.

Pros:
- Great visibility, you can see everything from the top mounted fans to the PSU cover on the bottom
- Very sturdy glass panels that are press-to-release (like your grandma's old curio cabinet doors)
- Compatibility with different sizes and configurations of case fans and radiators
- Airflow! There's so much room for airflow and the sides are all protected by mesh covers
- Sideways motherboard mounting gives a refreshing new look to an existing build
- Hidden compartment on the back of the top panel for wires to run to the back of the motherboard, makes for a very clean looking build
- Should fit almost any chonky or long GPU as long as you take one of the removeable metal coverings on the bottom off
- Has the option to buy add-ons such as a screen for the bottom front panel and a stand to display the case on its side

Cons:
- Standoffs are low quality and the holes for them may not be machined right, I had to replace many standoffs with extras I had and even then, some had to be forced into the holes because they hadn't been machined properly
- Back wiring can be an issue, especially if you have any kind of limited mobility in your hands. Lots of tight spaces, especially if you need to use the hard drive bay
- If you don't buy the add-on screen for the bottom front panel, you may see wires through the mesh depending on how you wired your system
- Very difficult to wire the PSU unless you have one with side-facing or angled connectors
- You can't have Wi-Fi antennas installed on the back of the motherboard with this case, they will not fit. If you have an antenna that sits away from the motherboard it will be fine, but antennas that come directly off the back of the motherboard will not fit. I suggest using Ethernet for this case
- Cannot put a radiator at the top of the case, only on the sides
- Will need a splitter for the USB ports on the front of the case for most motherboard models unless it has two inputs for case USBs

All in all, I'm really glad I bought this case even though the price made me feel a bit sick. I would not suggest it for beginners since the motherboard is rotated 90 degrees and can cause some issues with running wires, and the fans up top are a bit awkward. I can't attest to the fans that came with the case because I didn't use them, I already had case fans on hand that I used instead. Quality control on the hardware (screws, standoffs, etc) could be better but as long as you have extras on hand, it shouldn't be a big deal.

text:
I purchased this case after getting a 5090 and being concerned about its sheer weight of it hanging on the PCIe slot I knew there had to be a better way.

Ultimately I stumbled across this case with its unique rotated motherboard design and knew it was perfect.

Building:

Space - I found there to be plenty of room to adequately manage my cable runs and still have remaining room for airflow. My 5090 fits with enough space to not pinch the 12vhpwr cable. Also there are smaller magnetic plates on the back that allow you to run the cables through their channels.

Airflow - With the ability to have 3 120mm fans on the left and right side of the case both supporting a radiator should you want on top of space for 2 160mm fans on top and 2 160mm on the bottom, airflow is perfect. And I have to give a massive shout out to thermaltake for the fan trays making installation and maintenance simple. Along with thru included dust covers cleaning will be a breeze.

Best of all in my opinion is the tool-less maintenance panels. They are either magnetic or held in with a push to lock system.

Power supply… this is the one area I had the most difficulty with. There just isn’t enough space to accommodate the cables for the system. I feel like I had to stuff them in the bottom of the case. I have to highly recommend a modular supply as otherwise there will be too many cables in the way.

My only other complaint is how the cables that will be plugged into the motherboard for peripherals like mouse and keyboard are pretty tight. Not a huge concern but if you tend to plug and unplug a lot of things from your computer the front io is going to be the best bet.

This brings me to front io. With 4 usb 3.0 ports and 1 usbc port you really shouldn’t have difficulty with plugging things in. Lastly you have a headphone and microphone jack offering a wide array.

Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed building in this case and find it to be ascetically pleasing on the desk. It checked my major concern of fitting a 5090 and in a way I don’t have to worry about GPU sag. I highly recommend the case especially considering its price and will likely buy another for my Girlfriends computer.

text:
I know this case divides opinions but I am a big fan. I like the relatively simple look of it. The pattern of circles shown in the main photo for the item is actually a pattern on the mesh sheet; underneath, the metal itself has many small holes.

The case is pretty difficult to work in as the glass panel is your only real access point, but it was entirely manageable. I had to bend the rear GPU bracket back just a bit to accommodate my RX6600XT, but no big deal there either. The rear channel for cable management is a great addition, and the case itself has a nice paint/build quality.

The thermals for this case are excellent. Under worst stress conditions, I have not gotten anywhere close to thermal limits.

HOWEVER:

Note that a 240mm AIO will NOT fit on the top of the case; with the motherboard installed, the RAM will interfere with the AIO. I was able to install mine at the front of the case (make sure you do this with the radiator tube side down), but keep in mind that the thickness of your AIO will then cut into your CPU clearance. Generally, AIOs are around 50mm thick, so the 360mm GPU space becomes more like 310mm. Also, bear in mind that the case only comes with 1 fan, but fans are cheap so this is not a big deal. I installed two 120mm fans on the top of the case, kept the single fan on the rear, and installed one 120m fan on the bottom next to the power supply. This makes for excellent airflow, and the removable mesh panels make it very easy to manage dust.

Can't beat this case for the price!

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Overall? An excellent budget-friendly case that has everything you need with a very clean-looking design and compact size. I do have some nitpicky things regarding airflow but for budget-midrange builds this is perfect for a case under $60.

Pros: Clean aesthetic with 2 magnetic dust filters. Easy to build in and the lack of psu shroud allows for more air to circulate. Front IO is more than enough for budget in mind. Can support a 240mm aio in front if desired. Clean cutouts for cable management despite compact design.

Cons: Airflow is questionable. The dust filters have a hole printout design that makes the case look as if it has larger holes for airflow, but the actual holes behind the filter are significantly smaller. This caused temperatures to get higher than expected. For reference, I used an RX 6600 and an R5 5600 with a stock cooler. With 2 140mm fans in the front and 120 in the back for exhaust as well as a stock CPU cooler, my temps were reaching 80 degrees under load. After getting a cheap aftermarket cooler and adding 2 extra fans on top and bottom for intake, temps for GPU and CPU dropped to around 70 under load. After some tinkering with fan curves, I got an optimal fan noise to temperature ratio. If the holes on the actual case were the size of the dust filters, then I would have not needed to buy 2 extra fans and a tower cooler, luckily I had some budget to spare. Coolermaster, if you do a refresh of this case, please address airflow issues on the front intake panel. Doing so would make this, in my eyes the BEST budget case in the market.

All in all, I highly recommend this case, especially if you're on a budget. Just don't expect a 4090 and a 14th gen i9 to breathe here.

text:
This Rosewill Power Supply Unit (PSU) is very quiet, and is working well in my older Lenovo Ideacentre 430 that lost power to my SATA/SSD drives. I highly recommend viewing several YT videos for installation tips, especially on replacing cables one at a time (from old to new PSU), understanding the proper orientation of the cable connectors, and using proper precautions with sensitive electronic parts inside your computer. It looks nice and is well ventilated; it is actually physically shorter in length (all other dimensions were standard/as expected) than the older PSU it replaced, which made routing and managing cables for maximum air flow through the case much easier. I think it is a great value, saving me hundreds of dollars over a complete computer replacement. The PSU also arrived factory-packed in heavy-duty bubble wrap, which I think could protect the unit from all but the most extreme physical impacts.

I like semi-modular PSUs (like this one) best, because the hard-wired components are "must-haves" that are necessary for all PCs to run. The modular wires are plugged in only as-needed, helping keep the cooling airflow through your case maximized by installing minimizing cables to only those components needed for your specific computer's needs. The cables are marked for easy installation. Where modular cables are used, they plug into this PSU easily, but stay in place once fully inserted. The provided cable ties were a nice addition as well.

Recommended for do-it-yourselfers (or people who have computer savvy relatives/friends); it took just minutes from unplugging the old PSU from the wall to plugging my computer back into this PSU (including tying my cables up to optimize air flow through the case).

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
At $50, the 650W version is is a 5* supply for my low-midrange system, replacing a blown Corsair supply. Necessary cables were included, and the semi-modular design eliminated some unneeded ones. They're all 18 AWG, 90C -- a bit of overkill in some cases, and stiffer than the 20 and 22 AWG, 80C SATA and Molex cables from my old supply. The connectors were fine.

In Fig. 1, Rosewill is presumably scaling the load across all outputs. Under that assumption, the 115V efficiency Eff(percent) in terms of output power (P, watts) is roughly Eff = 95.4 - 700W/P - 0.0157xP. The Loss in watts would then be 7W + 0.0465xP + 0.000157xP^2.

Fig. 2 displays the cable connectors and capacities. ATX 3.x power supplies have shuffled current capacities: +3.3V and +5V are down to 18A -- but motherboards now power the CPU from +12V, instead of the +3.3V line. The -12V line is down from 0.8A to 0.3A. My ASRock B450m Pro4 motherboard is said to require -12V for the audio, though the ATX 3.x standard now has -12V as optional; 0.3A seems to suffice. And, of course, +12V current capacity is way up.

Note that both 6+2 pin PCIe connectors are on a single 2-ft. cable, plugging into a single power supply socket. At the 375W limit, that's 31.3A over 3 lines, effectively 10.4A through each pair of 4-ft, 18 AWG wires. The ampacity for an 18 AWG copper wire is nominally 18A at 90C, so that part is OK. At 65C, resistance is 7.51 ohm/1000 ft, giving a voltage drop of 0.31V and power loss of 9.7W for the 3 pairs... probably OK, but most modular ATX 3.1 supplies use multiple PCIe connectors and cables. The voltage drop is going to be a bit less for the PCIe 12+4 cable -- less than 600W through 6 pairs of 18 AWG wires.

Again, I don't expect any problems on a low-midrange system, but it's become hard to find detailed specs on motherboards, etc., so one doesn't know exact power supply requirements.
